9410:
To jingle means to make — or to cause to make — a light, gentle, high-pitched, repeating sound, like small metal objects repeatedly hitting against each other.

Think of what happens when you shake a handful of coins in your fist, or when someone with a bunch of keys walks down a hallway. That soft, rapid, musical clinking sound — that is a jingle. The objects are jingling.

Not every sound qualifies. The jingle sound has a very specific character:

  • Light and gentle — not loud, not deep, not heavy. A heavy iron gate clangs. Small coins jingle.
  • High-pitched — it sits in the bright, thin range of sounds, not the low, rumbling range.
  • Repetitive — it is not a single sound. It is a quick, continuous series of small sounds, one after another, because the objects keep moving and touching each other.
  • Metallic or bell-like — it comes from hard, small, light objects, most often made of metal. The sound has a bright, slightly musical quality to it.

Some objects are natural jinglers — whenever they move, they produce this sound:

  • Coins in a pocket or a purse — as you walk or reach inside, they jingle against each other.
  • Keys on a keyring — when you pick up the ring, shake it, or toss it on a table, it jingles.
  • Small bells — like the bells on a Christmas wreath, a cat's collar, or an anklet worn as jewellery. Any slight movement makes them jingle.
  • A charm bracelet — the small charms hanging from it hit each other and jingle when the wrist moves.
  • Spurs on a cowboy's boots — they jingle with every step.
  • Dog tags or pet collar tags — they jingle as the animal moves around.

Notice a pattern: these are all small, light, metal objects that are grouped together or dangling, so that movement causes them to repeatedly tap against each other.

1. The thing makes the sound on its own:

In this use, the subject of the sentence is the thing producing the sound.

"The coins jingled in her pocket as she walked."
"His keys jingled when he reached for the door."
"The tiny bells on the wreath jingled in the breeze."

Here, the coins, the keys, and the bells are the ones doing the jingling. No person is intentionally making it happen — it is a natural result of their movement.

2. A person makes something jingle:

In this use, a person deliberately shakes or moves an object to produce the sound.

"He jingled the coins in his hand nervously."
"She jingled her keys to get the dog's attention."
"The shopkeeper jingled the bell on the counter."

Here, a person is the one performing the action — they are intentionally making the object produce that sound.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Jingle" is not a neutral, blank word. It carries a certain mood with it.

It feels cheerful and light. It is associated with movement, energy, and often with pleasant occasions — the bells at a festival, coins in a full pocket, a playful pet running around the house. When you read that something is jingling, your mental image is lively, not gloomy.

Compare: if you read that "heavy chains clanked in the dark corridor," the feeling is heavy and ominous. But if you read that "little bells jingled over the bakery door," the feeling is warm and welcoming. The sound itself is the same basic type — metal hitting metal — but jingle specifically belongs to the lighter, brighter, friendlier end of that range.
How It Is Different from Similar Words

Since learners often confuse words that seem close in meaning, here is how "jingle" is distinct:

  • Clang / Clank — These are loud, heavy metallic sounds. A sword dropped on stone clangs. A jingle is the much lighter, softer, higher cousin of these words.
  • Ring — A ring is usually one sustained, clear tone (like a single bell being struck and held). A jingle is many quick, light sounds in fast succession.
  • Tinkle — This is very close to jingle. Both are light and high-pitched. The difference is subtle: a tinkle tends to be even softer and more delicate (like water dripping into a crystal glass, or a very tiny bell). A jingle implies a bit more energy, movement, and the sense of multiple objects touching each other rapidly. A single small bell might tinkle; a bunch of bells shaken together jingle.
  • Rattle — A rattle is also a series of rapid repeated sounds, but it sounds dry, hollow, and often somewhat unpleasant or alarming (like pills in a bottle, or bones). A jingle is specifically bright and metallic, never hollow.
In Context: Recognizing "Jingle" in Real Sentences

"I could hear him coming from the end of the hallway — his keys were jingling loudly with every step."

Here, the keys are making that bright metallic sound repeatedly as he walks.

"She sat in the waiting room, nervously jingling the change in her coat pocket."

She is moving the coins around with her hand, making them produce that sound — a sign of her nervousness.

"The old shopkeeper's door was fitted with a small bell, and it jingled every time a customer entered."

The bell, being struck by the door's movement, produces that light, repeating ring.

"The puppy came bounding in, its collar tags jingling merrily."

The tags (small metal ID plates on the collar) are hitting each other with each movement and producing that cheerful sound.

To jingle is to produce — or to make something produce — a light, bright, high-pitched, repeating metallic sound, caused by small objects (usually metal) moving and tapping against each other continuously.
9411:
Jingoism means an extreme, aggressive form of nationalism — a blind, passionate belief that your own country is superior to all others, combined with a strong desire to show that superiority through military force, threats, or an openly hostile attitude toward other nations.

Think of it this way: a patriot loves their country. A jingoist loves their country and wants their country to dominate, intimidate, or overpower others — and gets emotionally charged up about it.

To really understand jingoism, you need to see that it always combines three things together:

1. Extreme national pride bordering on arrogance. A jingoist doesn't just think their country is great — they think it is inherently superior to other nations, and they dismiss or look down upon foreign peoples, cultures, and governments without much thought or fairness.

2. Aggressive foreign policy. Jingoism is most clearly seen in how a country deals with the outside world. A jingoist strongly favors using military power, threats, or confrontation in international affairs. Diplomacy, compromise, and peaceful negotiation are seen as signs of weakness. The attitude is: "We are powerful. We don't negotiate — we demand."

3. Emotional, irrational fervor. Jingoism is not a calm, reasoned political position. It is fueled by hot emotion — fear of outsiders, wounded national pride, a hunger for glory, or a mob mentality stirred up by speeches, propaganda, or sensationalist media. A jingoist rarely stops to think critically about whether their country might be wrong in a given situation. They support their country the way a fanatic supports a sports team — unconditionally and aggressively.

This is the most important distinction to understand.

Patriotism is a genuine love and appreciation for your country. A patriot is proud of their nation's values, history, and people. They want their country to do well and do right. Importantly, a patriot can still acknowledge their country's faults and want to improve them.

Jingoism takes that love and twists it into something dangerous. It removes all self-criticism and replaces it with the attitude of "my country, right or wrong — and anyone who questions it is a traitor." It also adds outward aggression — the desire to flex military muscle and treat other nations as rivals to be beaten or enemies to be crushed.

In short: patriotism is inward love; jingoism is outward aggression dressed up as love.
What Jingoism Looks Like in the Real World

Jingoism shows up in many recognizable forms:

  • A government launching or threatening wars for reasons of national pride or glory, rather than genuine self-defense or justice.
  • Newspapers or media outlets publishing dramatic, exaggerated stories about foreign threats to whip up public anger and enthusiasm for war.
  • Politicians giving fiery speeches that portray their country as a great warrior-nation and foreign countries as dangerous enemies, in order to gain popular support.
  • A large segment of the population enthusiastically cheering for military action against another country, without much thought about the cost, the ethics, or whether the conflict is even justified.
  • The suppression of anti-war voices as "unpatriotic" or "treasonous."

A famous historical example is the media coverage in the United States before the Spanish-American War of 1898, where certain newspaper publishers ran sensationalized, often exaggerated stories about Spanish aggression in Cuba specifically to inflame public opinion and push the country toward war. That era is now considered a textbook case of jingoism in action.

Jingoism is always a negative, critical word. No one proudly calls themselves a jingoist. It is a label used by others to criticize or condemn a person, a government, a newspaper, or a movement for being recklessly, dangerously nationalistic. When someone calls a politician's speech "jingoistic," they are saying it is shallow, aggressive, and dangerously irresponsible — not a compliment.

• Jingoist (noun) — the person who practices jingoism. "He was a proud jingoist who believed every dispute with a foreign country should be settled by force."
  • Jingoistic (adjective) — used to describe something that has the quality of jingoism. "The senator's jingoistic rhetoric alarmed even members of his own party."
  • Jingoistically (adverb) — in a jingoistic manner. "The crowd jingoistically chanted for war."
How to Use "Jingoism" in a Sentence

• "The president's speech was pure jingoism — all bluster and threats, with no real strategy."
  • "Historians have criticized the era's journalism as jingoism disguised as news reporting."
  • "Jingoism is dangerous because it makes a population feel righteous about actions that are often reckless or unjust."
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Jingoism is the dangerous extreme of patriotism — where love of country turns into aggressive, irrational hostility toward other nations, and where military force is seen as the first and proudest answer to any international conflict.
9412:
A jingoist is a person who believes their own country is the greatest in the world — and, crucially, is ready and eager to use military force, aggression, or threats against other countries to prove it or protect it. It goes far beyond simply loving your country. A jingoist wants their nation to dominate, and they get almost excited at the idea of war or confrontation with foreign nations.

Think of it this way: a jingoist doesn't just feel proud of their country — they feel that their country is so superior that it has the right to bully, intimidate, or attack others. They tend to see diplomacy (talking things out peacefully) as weakness. In their mind, the best solution to any international problem is force, or at least a very loud threat of it.

A jingoist typically holds all of these beliefs at once:

My country is the best. Other countries are lesser, weaker, or inferior. If another country gets in our way, we should not negotiate — we should crush them. War is not a tragedy to be avoided; it is a tool to be used, even celebrated. Anyone who disagrees with this aggressive stance is a coward or a traitor.

This is what separates a jingoist from a regular person who simply loves their country. The jingoist's patriotism has curdled into something aggressive and dangerous.
The Crucial Difference: Patriot vs. Jingoist

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand, because people sometimes confuse the two.

A patriot loves their country deeply. They are proud of it, they defend it, they want the best for it. But they can also acknowledge when their country is wrong. They prefer peace over war when possible. They respect other nations' right to exist and govern themselves.

A jingoist has taken that love of country and twisted it into hostility toward the rest of the world. They cannot acknowledge any fault in their own country. They see other nations not as different, but as threats or obstacles. Their "love" of country is really less about love and more about a lust for national dominance.

A good way to remember this: Every jingoist is a patriot, but not every patriot is a jingoist. Jingoism is what happens when patriotism goes to an extreme and becomes aggressive.
What a Jingoist Looks and Sounds Like in Real Life

A jingoist might be a politician who constantly calls for military action against foreign countries and mocks any leader who tries to negotiate a peaceful solution. They might cheer when their country invades another, even if that war turns out to be unjust. They might say things like "We should just bomb them into submission" or "Why are we wasting time talking to these people? Show them who's boss." They dismiss suffering caused by their country's military actions as either deserved or unimportant.

A jingoist is often very loud about their views. They wrap themselves in national symbols — flags, slogans, anthems — and use those symbols as weapons to shame anyone who questions aggressive foreign policy. Criticise the war? To a jingoist, you are a traitor.
Is It a Compliment or an Insult?

It is always an insult, or at the very minimum, a very strong criticism. Nobody proudly calls themselves a jingoist. It is a label that others apply to someone to call out their reckless, aggressive nationalism. When you call someone a jingoist, you are saying: this person's love of their country has crossed the line into something ugly, irrational, and dangerous.
The Related Words You Should Know

Jingoism (noun) — the belief system or ideology itself. "The country was gripped by jingoism in the lead-up to the war." If jingoist is the person, jingoism is the philosophy they follow.

Jingoistic (adjective) — used to describe something that reflects or promotes this aggressive nationalism. "The newspaper ran jingoistic headlines that glorified the bombing." "His speech was jingoistic and irresponsible."

"The general was a jingoist who thought every border dispute was an excuse to deploy troops."

"She was no jingoist — she loved her country but believed war should always be the very last resort."

"The crowd cheered for the jingoist candidate who promised to make their enemies fear them."

"History has shown that jingoists rarely understand the true cost of the wars they so eagerly call for."

In short, a jingoist is someone whose national pride has become so extreme and so aggressive that it turns into a hunger for war and dominance over other nations. They are not merely proud citizens — they are cheerleaders for conflict, contemptuous of peace, and blind to their own country's faults. The word is always used critically, and rightly so, because throughout history, jingoism has been the attitude that has pushed nations into needless, destructive wars.
9413:
Jingoistic describes a person, attitude, speech, policy, or piece of writing that combines extreme pride in one's country with an aggressive desire for that country to dominate or threaten others, especially through military power.

It is always a negative word. Calling something jingoistic is a criticism, not a compliment. It describes a kind of dangerous, overheated nationalism — the kind that doesn't just love a country, but wants that country to bully, intimidate, or go to war with others.
Think of It as a Spectrum

To really understand "jingoistic," it helps to see where it sits compared to similar ideas:

Patriotic → Nationalistic → Jingoistic

  • Patriotic means you love your country. You feel proud of its history, culture, and people. This is generally seen as a warm, positive feeling. "I am proud to be from this country."
  • Nationalistic means you go a step further — you believe your country's interests should come before everything else, including cooperation with other nations. This is more self-centered, but not necessarily violent. "My country must always come first."
  • Jingoistic is the extreme end. It's not just pride or self-interest. It is the aggressive belief that your country is superior to others and should use its military strength to prove it or impose its will. "My country is the greatest, and we should crush anyone who gets in our way."

So jingoistic is patriotism that has gone wrong — that has curdled into aggression, arrogance, and warmongering.

A jingoistic attitude, speech, or policy typically has these qualities:

1. Blind, uncritical superiority
A jingoistic person doesn't just love their country — they believe it is simply better than all other countries, with no room for questioning or nuance. Any criticism of the home country is seen as betrayal.

2. Glorification of military strength
Jingoism loves the idea of a powerful military and sees war (or the threat of war) as something exciting, heroic, or necessary. A jingoistic speech might glorify soldiers and battle in a way that makes war sound desirable rather than tragic.

3. Hostility toward other nations
Jingoistic thinking tends to paint foreign countries as enemies, threats, or inferiors. It dehumanizes or dismisses other peoples and cultures.

4. Aggressive foreign policy
When a government acts jingoistically, it pushes for military solutions before diplomatic ones. It threatens, invades, or bullies other countries under the banner of "national greatness."

5. Loud, emotional, rally-the-crowd rhetoric
Jingoistic language is often dramatic and designed to stir up anger, fear, or aggressive pride — rather than to inform or reason with people.
Real-World Examples to Make It Concrete

• A politician gives a speech saying "We are the greatest nation on Earth, and any country that opposes us will face the full might of our military." That speech is jingoistic — it combines national superiority with military threats.
  • A newspaper covers a war by portraying the enemy country as monsters and celebrating every bomb dropped, without any concern for civilian lives on the other side. That coverage is jingoistic.
  • A government passes a policy that says, "We will expand our military bases into foreign territories to show the world who's in charge." That policy is jingoistic.
  • A crowd chants slogans calling for war against a rival nation just because of national rivalry, not because of any real threat. That crowd's behavior is jingoistic.

The word "jingoistic" carries a strong tone of disapproval and mockery. When a journalist, historian, or critic calls something jingoistic, they are saying:

"This is embarrassingly aggressive, dangerously simplistic, and driven by arrogance rather than reason."

It implies that the person or policy being described has let national pride completely override good judgment, compassion, and any serious thinking about the consequences of war or aggression.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "The general's jingoistic remarks alarmed diplomats who were trying to negotiate peace."
  • "The film was criticized for its jingoistic portrayal of the enemy nation as purely evil."
  • "Her jingoistic attitude made it impossible to have a balanced conversation about foreign policy."
  • "The rally's speeches were full of jingoistic fury, calling for military action without any thought of consequences."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly, remember this:

Jingoistic = aggressively and blindly proud of your nation in a way that promotes military force, hostility toward other countries, and the belief that your nation should dominate.

It is patriotism taken to a dangerous, warlike extreme — and the word is always used to criticize that extreme.
9414:
A jinx is a person, object, or invisible force that is believed to bring bad luck — not just once, but repeatedly, in a way that feels like more than coincidence.

The most important thing to understand right away is that a jinx lives in the world of superstition and belief, not proven science. Nobody can scientifically prove that a person or object "carries" bad luck. Yet the idea of a jinx is very real in everyday human thinking, because sometimes misfortune seems to follow a pattern so strong that people feel compelled to explain it.

A jinx can take three forms.

A person. Some people seem to bring misfortune wherever they go — every team they join loses, every project they touch falls apart, and accidents seem to follow them around. Such a person is called a jinx. For example: "Don't let Kevin come to the match — he's a jinx. Every single time he watches us play, we lose."

An object. A thing — a painting, a ring, a car, a house — can also be called a jinx if bad things keep happening around it or because of it. For example: "That old clock is a jinx. Ever since we brought it home, something keeps going wrong."

An invisible pattern or force. Sometimes there's no clear person or object to blame, but bad luck seems to be sitting over a situation like a dark cloud. In this case, people refer to the jinx as an unseen force. For example: "There's a jinx on this project — no matter how well we plan, something always goes wrong at the last moment."

This is what separates a jinx from ordinary bad luck.

Ordinary bad luck is a one-off event — you miss your train, you drop your phone. It happens, it's over, and you move on. A jinx, however, involves a streak — a repeated pattern of things going wrong in a way that starts to feel impossible to ignore. It makes people say, "This cannot just be a coincidence."

Think of it like this: if it rains on one picnic, that's bad luck. But if it rains every single time a specific person attends a picnic, people start calling that person a jinx.

The bad luck a jinx brings is also seen as having a source — the person, the object, or the invisible force — which makes it feel different from random misfortune. There's something to point to.

One of the most common uses of the noun in everyday speech is in phrases like "that's a jinx" or "don't jinx it." This reflects a widespread superstition: if you speak too confidently about a good outcome before it has actually happened, you might attract bad luck and cause it to fail.

For example, if your team is winning a game at halftime and someone says "We're definitely going to win today!", another person might say, "Don't say that — it's a jinx!"

The belief is that premature confidence or celebration invites misfortune. The noun "jinx" here refers to that act of tempting fate — saying the good thing aloud before it's certain is itself considered a jinx.
How Jinx Differs from Similar Words

Bad luck is general and has no source. It just happens randomly. A jinx, by contrast, has a perceived cause — something or someone to point at.

A curse is more serious and deliberate. In stories and folklore, someone intentionally puts a curse on another person, often through magic or a spoken declaration of ill will. A jinx, however, doesn't require any intention — it just passively seems to bring misfortune along with it.

A hex is very similar to a curse — usually a deliberate act of magical ill-wishing, strongly tied to ideas of witchcraft. Like a curse, it implies intent. A jinx is milder and far more common in casual conversation. You'd use "jinx" in a lighthearted or even playful tone; you'd use "hex" or "curse" in a darker, more serious context.

A rough scale: jinx (mild, everyday, no intent) → curse/hex (stronger, darker, usually intentional).

"Break the jinx" means to finally end a long streak of bad luck. Example: "The team broke the jinx after 15 years by finally winning the championship."

"Put a jinx on something" means to be the cause of its misfortune. Example: "I think you put a jinx on the trip by saying nothing could go wrong."

"There's a jinx on something" means that something seems to be under a cloud of persistent bad luck. Example: "There's definitely a jinx on that corner — three different businesses have opened there and all three have shut down."

"She/he is a jinx" is the most direct way to call a person a carrier of bad luck.

Jinx is not a dramatic or heavy word. It belongs to casual, everyday conversation. When someone calls a person a jinx, they are usually being a little playful or light-hearted — perhaps slightly superstitious — but rarely completely serious. It doesn't carry the dark, threatening weight of words like "curse" or "hex."

A jinx (noun) is a person, object, or unseen force believed to be the source of repeated bad luck. It is not about random, one-time misfortune — it is about a pattern of things going wrong that feels too consistent to be coincidence. It lives in the world of superstition and everyday belief, is used in a casual and conversational tone, and involves no deliberate intention to cause harm (unlike a curse or hex). The bad luck simply seems to follow it, like a shadow.
9415:
To jinx something or someone means to bring bad luck to it, or to cause something to go wrong, usually without meaning to. When you jinx something, you don't necessarily do anything physically harmful — the "damage" happens through superstition, fate, or bad luck that seems to follow.

Think of it this way: a jinx is like an invisible curse that you accidentally place on a person, a situation, or an event, making things go wrong when they were going well.

The word only makes sense if you understand the superstition it's built on: people believe that speaking too confidently about a good thing — or celebrating too early — can cause that good thing to fail.

It's the idea that luck is fragile. If you boast about it, announce it, or take it for granted, you might accidentally "break" it. This is irrational — most people know that — but the feeling is deeply human, which is why the word is used so widely.
The Two Main Ways "Jinx" Is Used as a Verb

1. To jinx someone or something by speaking too soon

This is the most common use. You jinx something when you say something confidently about a good outcome before it has actually happened, and then things go wrong.

"She said the surgery would go perfectly. She totally jinxed it — there were complications."

"Don't jinx it by saying we've already won. The game isn't over yet!"

Here, jinxing is caused by words — specifically by premature confidence or celebration. The person didn't do anything evil. They just spoke too soon, and bad luck followed (or so people believe).

2. To jinx someone simply by bringing bad luck around them

In a broader sense, you can jinx someone just by being near them or being involved with them in a way that seems to attract misfortune.

"Every team he plays for loses the championship. He jinxes every team he joins."

"I'm not inviting him to the launch. He jinxes everything."

Here, it's less about a specific statement and more about a pattern of bad luck that seems to follow a person.
The Most Famous Phrase: "Don't jinx it!"

You will hear this constantly in everyday English. It's what someone says when another person is being too optimistic or celebrating prematurely.

Friend A: "I'm definitely going to get that job. I can already feel it!"
Friend B: "Shhh! Don't jinx it!"

Friend B is warning Friend A: stop saying that out loud — you might cause it not to happen. It's a playful but genuine expression of superstitious caution.

Similarly, people say "You jinxed us!" to blame someone after something goes wrong, especially if that person was being overly confident beforehand.
Who Jinxes Whom? (The Grammar of It)

As a verb, "jinx" always needs a target — something or someone that is jinxed.

  • You jinx a person → "Stop talking like that, you're going to jinx me!"
  • You jinx an event → "He jinxed the wedding by predicting it would be flawless."
  • You jinx a team or group → "Don't put that banner up yet — you'll jinx the team."
  • You jinx a streak or situation → "She jinxed our winning streak."

"Jinx" is an informal, everyday word. You'd hear it in casual conversations, in sports commentary, among friends and family. It is not used in formal writing, legal language, or academic text.

It can be said playfully ("You jinxed it, you goofball!") or in genuine frustration ("I swear you jinxed this entire project."). The tone depends on the situation, but the word itself is never harsh or offensive.

It's important to separate "jinx" from similar-sounding ideas:

  • It is not a deliberate act of harm. Unlike a curse someone casts on purpose with malicious intent, jinxing is almost always accidental. Nobody means to jinx things — it just happens through careless optimism or bad luck.
  • It does not imply any supernatural power on the part of the person doing the jinxing. They aren't a witch or a villain. They're just someone who seems to attract misfortune.
  • It is not the same as a literal curse. Jinx is a casual, everyday word. Saying someone jinxed something is not a serious accusation — it's a light, often half-joking remark rooted in superstition.

To jinx something = to bring bad luck to it, usually by being too confident, celebrating too early, or simply being associated with misfortune. It is rooted in superstition, used in casual speech, and almost always describes something that happens by accident, not intent. The word is used both playfully and with genuine frustration, and it's one of the most common superstition-related words in everyday English.

Jitters means a feeling of nervousness, anxiety, or unease — the kind you feel right before something important, challenging, or unfamiliar happens.

Think of it as that restless, on-edge feeling in your body and mind when you are about to do something that makes you a little (or a lot) worried. Your stomach might feel tight, your hands might tremble slightly, your heart might beat a little faster. That whole bundle of feelings — that is the jitters.
A Key Thing to Know: It Always Comes With "The"
You almost never say "I have jitters." You say "I have the jitters." The word almost always travels with the word the in front of it. Keep this in mind — it is a fixed habit of the word.
Two Sides of the Same Word

Jitters carries two closely related meanings that often overlap:

1. The emotional/mental side — worry and nervousness about what is coming.

"She had the jitters all morning before her job interview."

This is the most common use. The person feels anxious, unsettled, and cannot fully relax because something stressful or exciting is ahead.

2. The physical side — shaking, trembling, or restlessness in the body.

"Two strong cups of coffee gave him the jitters."

Here, the word describes actual physical shakiness or an unsteady, jittery feeling in the body — often caused by too much caffeine, lack of sleep, stress, or similar things.

In real life, both sides usually happen together: you feel mentally anxious and your body reflects it through shaking or restlessness.
How It Is Used in Sentences

The word slots naturally into a few very common patterns:

"Have the jitters" — to feel nervous

"I always have the jitters before a big presentation."

"Get the jitters" — when the feeling comes over you

"He gets the jitters every time he has to speak in public."

"Give someone the jitters" — when something causes your nervousness

"Loud, sudden noises give her the jitters."
"The thought of flying gives me the jitters."
Common Phrases You Will Hear in Real Life

Because jitters is such a natural, everyday word, people often pair it with the situation causing the nerves:

  • First-day jitters — the nervousness you feel on the first day of a new school, job, or experience.
  • Pre-wedding jitters (or wedding-day jitters) — the anxiety a person feels right before getting married, even when they are happy about it.
  • Pre-game jitters — the nerves an athlete feels before a big match or competition.
  • Stage jitters — the nervousness a performer feels before going on stage (similar to "stage fright").

These phrases are used constantly in everyday English, so recognizing them will help you a lot.
Jitters in News and Financial Language

You will also see jitters used beyond personal feelings. In newspapers and news reports, writers use it to describe collective unease or uncertainty — when a large group of people, investors, or even an entire market feels anxious about something.

"Economic jitters spread across global markets after the unexpected announcement."
"Political uncertainty has caused jitters among investors."

Here, no single person has the jitters — instead, the word describes a widespread mood of worry or instability. This is a slightly more formal, extended use of the word, but the core idea (anxiety, unease) remains exactly the same.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Jitters is an informal, conversational word. It is perfectly fine to use in:

  • Everyday speech
  • Casual writing
  • Journalism and news articles
  • Storytelling and fiction

It would feel out of place in highly formal academic or legal writing, where you would instead use words like anxiety, apprehension, or nervousness. But in most real-world situations, jitters is widely understood and completely natural.
What Makes Jitters Different from Similar Words

• Nervousness is the general feeling. Jitters is a more vivid, physical, and informal way to say the same thing.
  • Anxiety can be long-lasting and deep. Jitters are usually short-term — they come right before an event and tend to go away once it begins.
  • Fear suggests a real danger. Jitters are more about anticipation and uncertainty than actual danger.
  • Butterflies (in your stomach) is a similar informal expression, but it is softer and often used for excitement mixed with nerves. Jitters leans a little more toward pure nervousness or unease.

Jitters are the nervous, uneasy, often slightly shaky feelings you get before something important or stressful — a vivid, informal word that captures both the mental anxiety and the physical restlessness that come with it.
9417: Jittery means feeling nervous, anxious, and restless — often in a way that shows up physically in your body. When you are jittery, your mind feels uneasy and on edge, and your body seems to reflect that unease too. Think of it as nervousness that you can feel and sometimes even see.
Breaking It Down: Mind and Body Together

What makes "jittery" special compared to simply saying "nervous" is that it captures both a mental feeling and a physical sensation at the same time.

Mentally, a jittery person feels:

  • Anxious and uneasy
  • Unable to relax or settle down
  • Tense and on edge, as if something bad might happen
  • Distracted and unable to focus

Physically, a jittery person might experience:

  • Shaky or trembling hands
  • A racing or pounding heart
  • Restlessness — they can't sit still, they fidget, they pace
  • A fluttery or unsettled feeling in the stomach (what people call "butterflies")

The two — mind and body — feed each other. The mental anxiety causes the physical shakiness, and the physical shakiness makes the anxiety worse.
What Causes Someone to Feel Jittery?

Understanding the causes of jitteriness will help you understand when and why this word gets used.

1. A stressful event coming up
Before a big exam, a job interview, a public speech, or a first date, people often feel jittery. The anticipation of something important — and the fear of things going wrong — creates that nervous, shaky feeling.

"She was jittery all morning before her driving test."

2. Too much caffeine
Caffeine (found in coffee, tea, and energy drinks) is one of the most common causes of literal, physical jitteriness. Too much of it makes your body feel wired, shaky, and restless, even if there's nothing to be afraid of.

"He drank four cups of coffee and spent the rest of the day feeling jittery."

3. Fear or a frightening experience
A sudden fright — hearing a loud noise, narrowly avoiding an accident, or being in a scary situation — can leave a person jittery long after the danger has passed. The body stays in a state of high alert.

"Even after the storm was over, the children were still jittery."

4. Uncertainty and unpredictability
When people don't know what's going to happen next — especially in dangerous or high-stakes situations — they become jittery. Soldiers before a battle, travelers in an unfamiliar and unsafe place, or anyone waiting for critical news can all feel jittery.

"The whole team was jittery as they waited for the results."

"Jittery" describes a moderate to significant level of nervousness. It's more intense than just feeling "a little uneasy," but it's not the same as pure terror or panic. Think of it as sitting somewhere in the middle of the nervousness scale — clearly uncomfortable, noticeably anxious, but still functional.

Low end: Slightly uneasy → a little nervous → jittery → very anxious → fearful → terrified
Can "Jittery" Describe Things Other Than People?

Yes — and this is an important nuance.

"Jittery" is often used to describe groups of people, animals, markets, and even situations — anything that shows signs of nervousness, instability, or unease.

  • Animals: Animals in the wild are naturally jittery because they are always on alert for predators. A deer, for example, is jittery — it twitches, looks around constantly, and runs at the slightest sound.

"The horses were jittery during the thunderstorm."

  • Markets and economies: In the world of finance and news, you will often hear that "the markets are jittery." This means investors are nervous and uncertain about the future, and as a result, stock prices are moving up and down unpredictably.

"The stock market has been jittery ever since the new regulations were announced."

  • Crowds or groups: A crowd of people waiting for uncertain news can collectively be described as jittery.

"The jittery crowd waited outside the hospital for hours."

Several words are close in meaning to "jittery," but each has a slightly different flavour. Understanding these differences will sharpen your understanding.

Nervous — the most general word for feeling worried or anxious. It doesn't necessarily imply any physical shakiness. "Jittery" is more intense and more physical than simply "nervous."

Anxious — focuses more on the mental worry about something in the future. You can be anxious while sitting perfectly still. "Jittery" adds the layer of physical restlessness that "anxious" doesn't always carry.

Edgy — means irritable and tense, ready to snap. An edgy person might react sharply to small things. "Jittery" focuses more on shakiness and nervousness; "edgy" focuses more on irritability.

Skittish — means easily startled or frightened, often used for animals or people who react nervously to small triggers. It's very close to "jittery" but leans more toward being easily spooked rather than a general state of anxiety.

Restless — means unable to stay still or relax, but without necessarily implying fear or nervousness. You can be restless out of boredom. "Jittery" always carries an element of anxiety.

On edge — an idiom (a set phrase) that means almost exactly the same as "jittery" — nervous, tense, and easily unsettled. You can use either one in most situations.

To further anchor the meaning, here is what "jittery" is the opposite of:

  • Calm — feeling peaceful and untroubled
  • Composed — in full control of one's emotions, especially under pressure
  • Relaxed — free from tension or worry
  • Steady — stable, not shaking, not easily disturbed
  • At ease — comfortable and free from worry
Common Patterns You'll See in Real Usage

Jittery pairs naturally with certain words. Here are the most common:

  • Feel jittery — "I always feel jittery before a presentation."
  • Get jittery — "She gets jittery whenever the phone rings late at night."
  • Make someone jittery — "The thunderstorm made the dog jittery."
  • A bit jittery / a little jittery — used to soften the intensity: "He was a little jittery, but he managed to get through the speech."
  • Jittery nerves — "The actor fought his jittery nerves before walking on stage."
One Final Way to Picture It

Imagine holding a cup of coffee with both hands — but your hands won't stop trembling. Your heart is beating a little too fast. Your eyes keep darting around. You keep shifting your weight from one foot to the other. You know there may be nothing to worry about, but your body refuses to believe it.

That feeling — that bundle of physical shakiness and mental unease — is what "jittery" describes perfectly.
9418: "Jive" as a verb has three distinct meanings in modern English. Knowing all three — plus one important note about a closely related word — will give you the complete picture.
Meaning 1: To be consistent or in agreement with something

This is the most common way "jive" is used as a verb today. When two things jive, they match, fit together, or make sense together. When they don't jive, they contradict or conflict with each other.

Examples:

  • "His story doesn't jive with the facts." → His story conflicts with the facts; they don't match.
  • "What she told me jives with what I already knew." → What she said is consistent with what I already knew — it fits.
  • "Something about his excuse just doesn't jive." → Something feels off or inconsistent about his excuse.
  • "The numbers in your report don't jive with the numbers in mine." → Our numbers contradict each other.

Think of it this way: two puzzle pieces either fit together or they don't. If they fit, they jive. If they clash, they don't jive.

This meaning is used constantly in everyday American English — in conversations, news articles, workplace discussions, and more.
Meaning 2: To talk in a teasing, exaggerated, or misleading way; to kid or fool someone

This is an older, informal/slang sense of "jive." When someone is jiving you, they are teasing you, messing with you, or not being straight with you. They might be exaggerating, being playfully deceptive, or just pulling your leg.

Examples:

  • "Stop jiving me — tell me the truth." → Stop messing around / stop misleading me.
  • "Are you jiving, or is that for real?" → Are you joking/teasing, or do you actually mean it?
  • "He was just jiving — he didn't mean it seriously." → He was just talking loosely/playfully, not being sincere.

You'll hear this less often in contemporary speech than Meaning 1, but it still appears, especially in older literature, films, and among older speakers.

"Jive" is also a style of energetic partner dance associated with swing and early rock and roll music. As a verb, to jive means to perform this dance.

Examples:

  • "They were jiving all night at the party." → They were dancing the jive all night.
  • "Can you jive?" → Do you know how to dance the jive?

This usage is more common in British and Australian English than in American English. In everyday speech, you're more likely to hear this in the context of dancing competitions or music events.

Here is something many learners (and even native speakers) don't know, and getting this right puts you ahead of most people.

There is another word — "jibe" — which is the older, technically "correct" word for Meaning 1 (to be consistent with something). It comes from sailing: when a sail shifts to align with the wind, it jibes — it comes into line. Over time, this sense of "coming into agreement" moved into everyday language.

So technically speaking:

  • "The story doesn't jibe with the facts" is the more traditionally correct phrasing.
  • "The story doesn't jive with the facts" is the version most people actually use today.

Because "jive" (meaning to be consistent) has become so widespread and natural-sounding, most modern dictionaries now accept it fully for this meaning. In casual and everyday speech, "jive" and "jibe" are interchangeable in this sense, and nobody will consider it an error.

However, in formal writing — think academic papers, legal documents, serious journalism — careful writers still prefer "jibe" for the "to be consistent with" meaning, and reserve "jive" for the slang/dance meanings.

Practical advice: In conversation and informal writing, freely use "jive" for all three meanings. In formal writing, use "jibe" when you mean "to be consistent with," and save "jive" for the teasing or dancing senses.
Quick summary of the three meanings

Jive = to be consistent with / to align with
→ "These two accounts just don't jive."

Jive = to tease, mislead, or kid someone
→ "Don't jive me — is it true?"

Jive = to dance the jive
→ "She jived beautifully at the competition."

One final thing worth knowing: in all three meanings, "jive" carries a slightly informal, casual tone. You wouldn't typically hear it in very formal or stiff language. It belongs naturally to everyday speech and writing.
9419:
Jobbery means the corrupt practice of using a position of public trust or official power to secretly serve private interests — your own, or those of your friends, allies, or financial backers — instead of serving the public good you were supposed to serve.

Think of it this way: when someone is given a powerful role — say, a government minister, a senior official, or a committee head — the public trusts them to use that role fairly and honestly. Jobbery is when they betray that trust by quietly turning their official power into a tool for personal profit or private benefit.

Jobbery is not just general dishonesty. It has a specific shape. It almost always involves the corrupt distribution of something valuable — such as:

  • Jobs and appointments — filling public positions with unqualified friends, political allies, or people who have paid for the favour, rather than the most deserving candidates.
  • Government contracts — awarding lucrative contracts to a friend's company or a business partner, not because they offered the best service or price, but because of the private relationship.
  • Licences, grants, or privileges — using official authority to hand out valuable permissions or public money to those who have something to offer in return.

The defining feature in every case is the behind-the-scenes private deal — the official acts as though they are doing their public duty, but the real motive is private gain.

Imagine a government official is in charge of awarding a large contract to build public roads. Three companies submit bids. Fairly, the contract should go to the company offering the best quality at the best price. But this official secretly awards the contract to his old friend's company — a company that made a generous donation to his political campaign and promised him future business opportunities. The public loses. The friend gains. The official gains. That is jobbery.
The Key Elements That Must Be Present

For something to qualify as jobbery, these three things need to be true:

  1. There is a position of power or trust involved. The person committing jobbery has been given authority — over jobs, contracts, public resources, appointments, or similar things of value.
  2. That authority is misused. Instead of using it fairly and in the public interest, the person uses it to serve a hidden private agenda.
  3. There is personal or private gain. Someone benefits privately — whether it's the official themselves, their family, their friends, their political backers, or anyone with a private relationship to the official.

If any of these elements is missing, it may be a different kind of wrong — but it isn't jobbery in the precise sense.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close neighbours, and people sometimes use them loosely, but they are not identical:

  • Corruption is the broad, umbrella term for dishonest or illegal behaviour in a position of power. Jobbery is a specific type of corruption — one that centres on the misuse of a position to hand out patronage and privilege privately.
  • Nepotism is the specific act of favouring family members — hiring your cousin, promoting your sibling. Jobbery is wider. It doesn't have to involve family; it can involve friends, donors, allies, or anyone the official has a private interest in benefiting.
  • Cronyism is very similar and often used interchangeably with jobbery in casual speech, but cronyism specifically refers to favouring close friends or associates. Jobbery emphasises the transactional and official nature of the corruption more strongly — the misuse of a formal position to distribute public resources or appointments corruptly, often with something in return.
  • Bribery is about the exchange of money or gifts to influence someone's decisions. Jobbery may involve bribery, but it doesn't have to — a politician might commit jobbery simply by appointing a political ally without any money changing hands. The focus of jobbery is on the corrupt outcome (who gets the job, the contract, the privilege) rather than on the mechanics of the payment.
The Setting Where This Word Lives

Jobbery is a word rooted in public life and politics. You will most often encounter it in discussions of:

  • Government and political corruption
  • Public procurement and contracting scandals
  • The history of political patronage systems (where political parties handed out government jobs to their supporters as rewards)
  • Institutional or organisational corruption more broadly

It is a somewhat formal and serious word. You are more likely to read it in a newspaper editorial, a history book, a political essay, or a legal or academic context than to hear it in everyday conversation. It carries a tone of moral condemnation — to accuse someone of jobbery is to say that they have betrayed the public trust in a calculated, self-serving way.
The Spirit of the Word — Summed Up Simply

If you want one sentence to carry the meaning of jobbery with you forever:

Jobbery is the corrupt practice of quietly using public power as a private favour machine — handing out jobs, contracts, and privileges not on merit, but on the basis of personal relationships and private gain.

It is the story of someone who was given power to serve the many, and chose instead to serve the few — usually starting with themselves.
